title: A new valuation after every change
outcomes: Names the fact that changed after an exchange or a pawn move
Checks whether the old plan relied on that fact
Keeps the plan when nothing it relies on has changed
Picks a new plan from the new position when the old one is out of date

steps.text: A plan is a guess about one position. When the position changes (an exchange, a pawn move, a threat), the guess may be out of date. After each change ask two questions: **what changed?** and **did my plan rely on it?** If yes, make a fresh valuation, as a spectator would, and pick the plan again. If no, carry on. Changing plans when nothing changed wastes time.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has just played ...d6. White's plan was e5.

line.say: dxe5: the new pawn on d6 takes it.

claims.statement: The pawn on d6 attacks e5.
e5 is at least 200 cp worse than the best move.

steps.text: A change matters when it touches a fact the plan needs: a square, a piece, a file, a defender. Here the plan needed e5 free of pawn attacks. A king step or ...h6 touches none of these, but check each move: even a far pawn can hit a piece (...c5 attacks a knight on d4). Ignoring a real change is *thinking inertia*; reacting to an irrelevant one wastes time.

steps.prompt: White's plan is e5. The first board shows Black's reply ...h6: the plan stands. Now predict what happens to the plan after ...d6 and after ...Kh8, then check.
